newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Possible rate hike keeps Dutch dealers alert.
newsitem.headline: Possible rate hike keeps Dutch dealers alert.

text.p: Money market dealers remained divided over the possibility of a rate hike later today when the Dutch central bank sets a new special advances pact, though some said a 10-basis-point rise had already been priced in.
Some dealers said the weaker guilder versus the mark and a recent step-by-step increase in short-dated money market rates could trigger an increase in the special advances rate.
The special advances rate -- roughly equivalent to Germany's repo rate -- is the benchmark for all Dutch money market rates and has been pegged at 2.50 percent since August.
Dealers said an increase of 20 basis points in the special advances rate would push money market rates even higher.

"I think there's a 50/50 chance that the central bank will raise the special advances rate," said one dealer, adding that an increase of 20 basis points could prompt a rise in the secured loans rate. "But that seems unrealistic," he added.

A rise in the central bank's secured loans rate -- roughly equivalent to Germany's discount rate -- would be far more significant as commercial banks use this as a benchmark for their long-term loans to customers.
The guilder regained some ground against the mark today, but the Dutch currency remained relatively weak as it was trading at 112.415 per 100 marks versus 112.46 on Wednesday.
"A move by the central bank is very well possible as long as the market has to pay over 112.40 guilders per 100 marks," said another dealer.
Most business was done in deposits up to six months and dealers also noted interest for DTCs, short-term borrowing programmes of the Dutch government.
The two new DTC issues, with maturity dates of May 30 and December 31 were priced at respectively 3.07 and 3.16 percent, dealers said.
"Current price levels (for DTCs) are interesting so I am warmly recommending them to my clients," said one dealer.
Call money was bid at 2.75 percent, well below yesterday's 3.06 percent, but one-month deposits edged up further to 3.06 percent bid from 3.04 percent.
